questions.q: In physics, how do the terms distance and displacement differ?
options: Distance is the total length of the pathway taken and is a scalar; displacement is the change in position relative to the starting location and is a vector with magnitude and direction
Distance is a vector with direction; displacement is a scalar with magnitude only
Distance and displacement are interchangeable terms for the same quantity
Distance always has a direction associated with it; displacement never does
questions.explanation: Distance describes the total length of the pathway taken between the starting and finishing points and is a scalar (magnitude only). Displacement indicates the location of the destination relative to the start, irrespective of the path, and is a vector with both magnitude and direction.

questions.q: Of the quantities distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration, which are vector quantities?
options: Distance and speed only
Displacement, velocity and acceleration
Speed, velocity and acceleration
All five are vector quantities
questions.explanation: Distance and speed are scalar quantities (magnitude only). Displacement is the vector form of distance, velocity is the time rate of displacement and is a vector, and acceleration is the rate at which an object changes its velocity and is also a vector quantity.

questions.q: From memory: define average speed and average velocity, and state which is a scalar and which is a vector.
keyPoints: Average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the time taken, and is a scalar quantity.
Average velocity is the total displacement divided by the journey time (v_av = s/t), and is a vector quantity.
The average velocity vector acts in the same direction as the displacement vector.
questions.explanation: Average speed = distance/time (scalar); average velocity = displacement/time (vector, in the direction of the displacement). If you recalled both formulas and the scalar-vs-vector split, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: A champion swimmer completes 30 laps of a 50 m swimming pool, a distance of 1500 m, in a time of 15 minutes. What is their average velocity in m s⁻¹?
questions.given: distance = 1500 m,  number of laps = 30 (even),  t = 15 min = 15 × 60 s
working: Average velocity \(v_{av} = \dfrac{s}{t}\), where \(s\) is the total displacement.
30 laps is an even number, so the swimmer finishes at the starting wall.
questions.explanation: Velocity depends on displacement, not distance. After 30 laps the swimmer is back where they started, so the displacement and hence the average velocity are zero — even though the average speed is 1500/900 = 1.7 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: Convert a speed of 60 km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹.
questions.given: speed = 60 km h⁻¹;  1 km = 1000 m,  1 h = 3600 s
working: In effect, divide the speed in km h⁻¹ by 3.6.
questions.explanation: To convert km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹, divide by 3.6 (multiply by 1000/3600). So 60 km h⁻¹ = 16.7 m s⁻¹. To go the other way, multiply by 3.6.

questions.q: Acceleration is the rate at which an object changes its velocity. In what direction does the acceleration of an object act?
options: Always in the direction of the object's motion
Always opposite to the object's velocity
In the same direction as the change in velocity
Acceleration is a scalar and has no direction
questions.explanation: Because velocity is a vector, acceleration is also a vector quantity. The direction of the acceleration of an object is the same as the direction of its change in velocity, where the average acceleration a_av = Δv/Δt.

questions.q: A car starts from rest and reaches a velocity of 20 m s⁻¹ due east in 5.0 s. What is its average acceleration?
questions.given: u = 0,  v = 20 m s⁻¹ due east,  t = 5.0 s
questions.explanation: The change in velocity is found by subtracting the initial velocity u from the final velocity v. Here Δv = 20 m s⁻¹ east, and dividing by 5.0 s gives 4.0 m s⁻² due east — the acceleration points in the same direction as the change in velocity.

questions.q: On the velocity-versus-time graph of an elevator, during interval G the acceleration is positive (up) while the velocity is negative (down). What does this illustrate?
options: A positive acceleration always means the object is speeding up
The direction of the acceleration is the same as the direction of the change in velocity, which can be opposite to the velocity itself
The acceleration must be zero whenever the velocity is negative
The elevator must be momentarily at rest
questions.explanation: The direction of the acceleration is the same as the direction of the change in velocity. During interval G the elevator is moving down (negative velocity) but slowing/reversing, so the change in velocity — and hence the acceleration — points up. The sign of acceleration is a direction, not automatically 'speeding up'.

questions.q: From memory: what is the golden rule of the sign convention for one-dimensional motion, and why does it matter?
keyPoints: In a straight line a vector has only two possible directions, so a plus or minus sign replaces arrows and angles.
Choose one direction to be positive at the start of the problem, state it, and stay consistent throughout.
Most sign errors in kinematics come from quietly switching the convention partway through a problem.
questions.explanation: Pick a positive direction, declare it, and commit to it. A velocity of −5 m s⁻¹ simply means 5 m s⁻¹ in the negative direction. If you recalled 'choose, state, stay consistent', grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: An object is moving in the negative direction and has a negative acceleration. What is happening to its speed?
options: It is slowing down, because the acceleration is negative
It is speeding up, because the acceleration points the same way as the motion
Its speed is unchanged, because both are negative
It is momentarily at rest
questions.explanation: A negative acceleration means the acceleration points in the negative direction — it does not automatically mean 'slowing down'. Here the object already moves in the negative direction, so the acceleration is in the same direction as the motion and the object speeds up. Always check the direction of travel before reading the sign.

questions.q: Distinguish between distance and displacement, using the example of an athlete running one complete lap of a 400 m track. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: Distance is a scalar quantity that measures the total length of the path travelled by an object, and it has magnitude only. Displacement is a vector quantity that measures the change in position of an object from its starting point to its finishing point, and it has both magnitude and direction. An athlete who runs one complete lap of a 400 m track travels a distance of 400 m but has a displacement of zero, because they finish at their starting position.

criteria.descriptor: Names distance as a scalar and displacement as a vector (with direction).
Defines distance as total path length and displacement as the change in position from start to finish.
Uses the 400 m lap example: distance 400 m, displacement zero.

questions.explanation: Full marks require naming the scalar/vector type, stating that displacement has direction, and clinching the difference with the lap example where distance is 400 m but displacement is zero.
